title: System Prompts and Reusable Prompt Templates for Claude
titleVi: Chỉ dẫn hệ thống và mẫu câu lệnh tái sử dụng cho Claude

units.text: Design system prompts, templates, and guardrails
What you will be able to do
Set a role for Claude in the system prompt and explain why that is the main job of a system prompt
Write instructions that state the reason behind each constraint, and use numbered steps where order or completeness matters
Build a reusable template from a role, XML-tagged variable inputs, rules, scenario responses and a defined output format
Spot where an older consistency technique (prefill) no longer applies to current models
Key concept
Role-first system prompt

The system prompt is mainly where you set Claude's role, meaning who it is and what it is for. Rules, scenarios and output formats are added on top of that role, and a single sentence of role already changes Claude's behaviour and tone.
In this lesson
Start the system prompt with a role
Write instructions that are specific and give the reason
Turn the prompt into a reusable template
Start the system prompt with a role
In the Messages API, a system prompt goes in the
parameter, separate from the

array where the user's turns go. The guidance on what to put there is short: give Claude a role. Anthropic's prompting best practices say that setting a role focuses Claude's behaviour and tone for your use case, and that even a single sentence makes a difference. A role like "a helpful coding assistant specializing in Python" tells Claude which domain to draw on and which register to answer in, before the user has said anything.

The role also keeps behaviour steady over time. The output-consistency guidance tells you to use system prompts to define Claude's role and personality, because this "sets a strong foundation for consistent responses." This matters most in role-based applications such as a support bot or an internal assistant, where users expect the same character on every turn. Even system prompts built for other goals, such as protecting confidential instructions, are described as still being mostly role prompts. Everything else in the system prompt builds on that role.

Write instructions that are specific and give the reason

Once the role is set, the system prompt holds the instructions. The first principle is to be specific about the output format and constraints you want. Claude does what you ask, so if you want more you have to ask for it. "Create an analytics dashboard" gets you a dashboard. Adding "Include as many relevant features and interactions as possible. Go beyond the basics" gets you the fully-featured version. When the order or completeness of steps matters, write the instructions as a numbered or bulleted sequence rather than a paragraph.
Predict first
Your app reads Claude's responses aloud through a text-to-speech engine, and ellipses break it. Which instruction do Anthropic's docs present as more effective?
NEVER use ellipses
Your response will be read aloud by a text-to-speech engine, so never use ellipses since it will not know how to pronounce them.
Do not use ellipses under any circumstances. This is critical.

The second principle is to give the reason. Explaining why a behaviour matters helps Claude understand your goal and target its response. A rule with a reason covers more cases than the rule alone. If Claude knows the output goes to a speech engine, it can also avoid other things that engine can't pronounce, not only the one you listed. Guardrail wording in a system prompt works best the same way: state the rule and the reason for it, and wrap it in a descriptive tag so it reads as a separate block of policy. Anthropic publishes reusable snippets in this form, like the one below for reducing hallucinated claims about code.
A reusable system-prompt snippet: a behavioural rule wrapped in its own descriptive XML tag
xml
Exam trap
A capitalised absolute rule like "NEVER use ellipses" is the strongest way to word a constraint.
Why is that wrong?

When do the docs recommend writing instructions as numbered steps or bullet points instead of a paragraph?
When the order or completeness of the steps matters
Only when the prompt is longer than 20k tokens
Only inside the user turn, never in the system prompt
Always, because Claude ignores instructions written as paragraphs

Turn the prompt into a reusable template

A production prompt is a template. The fixed parts (role, rules, expected behaviour) stay the same, and the variable parts (the user's query, retrieved data) change on every request. XML tags keep these parts separate. The best-practices guide says tags help Claude read prompts that mix instructions, context, examples and variable inputs, and that putting each kind of content in its own tag reduces misinterpretation. Use the same descriptive tag names across all your prompts so that every template in your system follows the same structure.
A role-based template: role, a tagged variable slot, rules, and scripted responses for common scenarios
text

The last block in that template follows the docs' advice to provide a list of common scenarios and expected responses. That list prepares Claude for different situations so it doesn't break character. It also shows that a scripted reply works as a guardrail: when a user asks about protected IP, Claude has an exact sentence to use instead of making one up.
The building blocks of a reusable template, as shown in Anthropic's consistency examples

The structure of every response

Templates also fix the shape of the output. Define the format you want precisely, in JSON, XML or a custom template, and Claude will follow every formatting element you require. Examples are among the most reliable ways to set format, tone and structure. They should be relevant to your real use case and varied enough that Claude doesn't copy unintended patterns. Wrap them in
tags (and several in
) so Claude can tell them apart from instructions. For chatbots and knowledge bases, add a tagged block of retrieved entries (for example, a

section) to ground answers in a fixed information set. Older consistency advice also suggests prefilling the Assistant turn with the start of the format. Prefilling is not supported on Claude 4.6 and later models or on Claude Mythos Preview, so a template meant for current models should get its format from instructions and examples instead.
Exam trap
Prefilling the Assistant turn is a dependable way to enforce a template's output format on any Claude model.
Why is that wrong?
Checkpoint 3 of 4
Exam question

A team is building a customer support assistant and wants the system prompt to reliably shape Claude's tone and behavior across thousands of daily conversations. The current system prompt is a single sentence: "You are a helpful assistant." Support agents report inconsistent formality and occasional off-topic tangents. What is the most effective first change to the system prompt design?
Give Claude a specific role describing the product, audience, and tone, since even a one-sentence role framing measurably focuses behavior and register
Move all behavioral guidance into the first user turn instead, since system prompts have less influence on tone than user messages do
Replace the system prompt with a list of banned phrases only, since negative constraints are more reliable than positive role framing for tone
Increase the max_tokens parameter so Claude has more room to self-correct its tone mid-response after drifting off topic
